What to offer specifically: emergency cover, short-notice feeding, walks during a bad week, and looking after an animal during a hospital stay.

It's also worth agreeing what happens in the genuine worst case - if someone is taken to hospital suddenly, who has the key and who takes the animal. Uncomfortable to discuss, enormously reassuring once settled.

title: Throw A Thank You Party For Someone Who Deserves One
hook: Organise a surprise gathering for the person who quietly holds something together and has never once been thanked properly.
why: Every group has someone who does the invisible work - the person who books the pitch, runs the group chat, organises the rota, checks on everyone. They're thanked in passing and never properly. Gratitude that's specific, public and organised by other people is rare, and it lands very differently from a card. Most such people have genuinely never had it.
instructions:
Pick the person who quietly holds something together. A club secretary, a coach, a group chat organiser, a neighbour who checks on everyone, a colleague who covers for people, a friend who's been the reliable one for years.

Then organise something for them, without them having to do anything.

Making it land:
- Get the people they've actually helped, not just their friends. Reach is the point - hearing from twelve people they helped over a decade is what makes it work.
- Collect specific memories in advance. Ask everyone for one concrete thing this person did, and read them out or put them in a book. Specifics beat speeches.
- Make it clear it's for them and about them, right at the start. People like this deflect instinctively, and if you let them they'll spend the evening organising it.
- Keep it appropriate to the person. A loud surprise party is some people's nightmare - for others a quiet dinner with eight people they love is exactly right. Ask someone who knows them well.

Also worth doing at the same time: write to whoever's above them if it's a work or club context, so the recognition exists somewhere formal too.

You don't need an occasion, a retirement or a milestone. Doing it for no reason at all is what makes it memorable.

title: Run A Clothes And Style Exchange
hook: Everyone brings what they never wear, and the group works out what actually suits each other. Free wardrobe, no shopping.
needs: Clothes you don't wear, a mirror
why: Fast fashion is a major source of waste and emissions, and most wardrobes contain a large proportion of items that are never worn. Swapping directly keeps clothes in use and costs nothing. There's also a genuine confidence element - plenty of people avoid clothes they'd suit because nobody's ever told them, and honest friendly feedback is hard to come by.
instructions:
Everyone brings clothes they don't wear - wrong size, never suited them, bought and regretted, or just bored of. Lay it all out, put music on, and spend an evening trying things on and swapping.

How to run it well:
- Say clean and in good condition. This isn't a rubbish disposal route.
- Get a full-length mirror somewhere with decent light.
- Group things roughly by type rather than by whose they were - people are far more willing to try something when it isn't obviously being handed to them.
- Agree what happens to leftovers before you start, and take them straight to a charity shop or a shelter that same week. Otherwise they sit in someone's hallway for a year.

The advice half:
- Be honest but kind, and only when asked. Nobody wants an unsolicited critique of their existing wardrobe.
- Focus on what works rather than what doesn't. "That colour is brilliant on you" is more useful than a list of failures.
- Encourage people to try things they'd never pick. That's where the surprises are, and it's the entire advantage of doing this in a group.
- Be conscious that clothes and bodies are a sensitive combination for a lot of people. Keep it light, never comment on size or shape, and make sure there's somewhere private to change.

Works especially well before a season change, or for anyone starting a new job.

title: Run A CV And Interview Practice Night
hook: Spend an evening rewriting each other's CVs and running mock interviews - the help that's normally expensive or unavailable.
why: Career help is distributed almost entirely through networks, which is precisely why it compounds existing advantage - people with well-connected friends get feedback and introductions, and people without them don't. Practising an interview once before doing it for real measurably changes performance, and it costs nothing except a few people's evening.
instructions:
Get a group together, bring laptops and printed CVs, and work on each other's job applications properly.

A structure that works:
- Start with CVs. Swap with someone who doesn't know your industry - if they can't tell what you actually do within thirty seconds, neither can a recruiter.
- Then cover letters, which almost everyone writes badly and nobody gets feedback on.
- Then mock interviews in pairs, with a third person watching and taking notes. Use real questions from an actual job posting.
- Finish with LinkedIn profiles and, if anyone's up for it, practising how to ask for an introduction.

What makes the feedback useful:
- Be specific and structural, not encouraging. "This says you're a team player but never shows it" helps; "looks great" doesn't.
- Have people say their answers out loud rather than describing them. The gap between what you plan to say and what comes out is the whole point of practising.
- Look for buried achievements. Most people massively undersell themselves and need someone else to spot it.
- Let whoever has hiring experience lead that section - they know what actually gets read.

Extend the invitation beyond your immediate group: a neighbour's teenager, someone recently made redundant, a friend of a friend changing careers. Those are the people for whom this is worth the most and who are least likely to ask.

title: Do A Home Energy Audit Together
hook: Spend an afternoon going room by room finding draughts and waste - lower bills, lower emissions, and it costs nothing.
why: Household heating is a major source of emissions, and much of it escapes through gaps that cost a few pounds to seal. The barrier is knowing what to look for. Doing it as a group means one person's knowledge covers several homes at once - and the savings are real and immediate, which is unusual for anything climate-related.
instructions:
Go round each other's homes in turn, or do one together and take notes for the rest. Having several people looking is genuinely better - people are blind to their own house.

What to check:
- Draughts: letterboxes, keyholes, under doors, around window frames, unused chimneys, loft hatches, gaps in floorboards and around pipework. Draught-proofing strips cost very little and pay for themselves quickly.
- Loft insulation depth. This is one of the biggest single factors and lots of homes have less than recommended.
- Hot water cylinder jacket and pipe lagging, both cheap and frequently missing.
- Radiators: bleed them, check nothing is blocking them, and consider reflective panels on external walls.
- Boiler and thermostat settings. A lot of systems run hotter than necessary. Look up the correct flow temperature for your boiler type.
- Standby power - the devices left on constantly.
- Lighting still on halogen or incandescent bulbs.
- Curtains and where heat is escaping through glazing at night.

Then check what support exists. Most countries have grants, free insulation schemes or subsidised assessments, often income-linked, and they're chronically underclaimed.

Take photos and write an actual list for each home, prioritised by cost and impact. Otherwise it's an interesting afternoon that changes nothing.

Then go and help each other fit the draught strips.

title: Run A Plastic-Free Picnic
hook: Everyone brings food with zero single-use plastic. Harder than it sounds, and you'll learn a lot about what you buy.
why: Most household plastic use is invisible until you try to avoid it - it turns out to be nearly everything, and that realisation changes shopping habits more effectively than any amount of general advice. Doing it as a challenge with friends makes the learning concrete and shared, rather than an individual exercise in guilt.
instructions:
Everyone brings a dish to a picnic, with one rule: no single-use plastic anywhere. Not in the packaging you bought it in, not in how you transport it, not in the cutlery.

You'll immediately discover this is much harder than expected. That's the point.

What tends to work:
- Buy loose fruit and vegetables, and bring your own bags
- Bakery bread in paper, or bake it
- Cheese and meat from a counter into your own container - most will do this if you ask, though some will refuse
- Glass jars, beeswax wraps, tins and reusable containers for transport
- Proper cutlery and cloth napkins from home
- Drinks in glass, cans or a big refillable container rather than individual bottles

Make it a challenge rather than a rule. Compare notes on what was impossible, where you had to compromise, and which shops made it easy. The conversation is more valuable than the picnic.

Things people usually learn: that "recyclable" plastic often isn't recycled in practice, that most bulk stores are cheaper than expected, that the biggest offenders are snacks and anything pre-prepared, and that asking a butcher or deli to use your container is far less awkward than anticipated.

Take everything home. A plastic-free picnic that leaves anything behind has rather missed the point.
